chapter: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
title: The Kentucky Club: floor show, crowds and Paul Whiteman
summary: The band moves to the Kentucky Club at 49th and Broadway, packed after 3 a.m., with Whiteman and others sitting in on the floor.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Kentucky, that's the club. Kentucky Club, right on the corner of 49th and Broadway, Howard Johnson or somebody's got it now, down in the basement. This is prohibition, you know, 20's, 1921. I think it was '21 or something like that. So anyway we went down there, they had the floor show, the floor show, Dennis Hopper put on the show, had a comedian, Johnny Hodgins and Joe Smith played trumpet for him. We had a white master of ceremonies, he played piano, and had a white lady that sang, sang opera and all that crap. High tone. And a guy named Burt, he knew a thousand songs. Any song you'd name, he knew it, he'd play it.

But they would go on between the shows. Now, we played down there, and the word spread there's a different band in town. They sound different. Paul Whiteman was playing around the corner, had his band around the corner at the place there. Up the street was the Roseland Ballroom, Fletcher and them up there, all activities right around there, so

anyway at night those guys would get off early. We didn't go to work till 11:00 and we stayed open till 7:00 in the morning, anyway, our club was a little small place and after 3:00 in the morning you couldn't get a seat. They'd stand around and it got so popular, we were packed and jammed. Paul Whiteman would bring all his friends and band down there. But it was so small, a lot of times the guys would want to sit in and play with the band, but they had to sit on the floor. The floor was so crowded you couldn't dance.
The Club Kentucky was something and the money flying. Money is flying. Partner, the money is flying. You believe it. Now that's the 20's when a dollar was a dollar. Ain't nothing now.
